Central Nervous System
Physiology
Internal Capsule, UMNL, LMNL, Basal Ganglia

Quick Overview

This lesson covers the motor neurons of the spinal cord, then the internal capsule (its structure, fiber content and blood supply). It goes on to upper and lower motor neuron lesions, comparing their clinical features. It ends with the basal ganglia: their functional anatomy, connections, functions, lesions, and the distinction between rigidity and spasticity.

Complete Lesson Content

Motor neurons of the spinal cord (efferent neurons)

They occupy mainly the lateral and anterior horns of the spinal cord:

  • Large alpha cells: innervate extrafusal fibers of skeletal muscles; about 70% of anterior horn cells.
  • Gamma cells: innervate intrafusal fibers; relatively smaller; about 30% of anterior horn cells.
  • Lateral horn cells: give origin to the autonomic nervous system.

Internal capsule

Definition: a mass of white fibers, V-shaped in horizontal section, limited laterally by the lentiform nucleus of the basal ganglia and medially by the caudate nucleus and the thalamus.

Function: its fibers connect the higher centers in the cerebral cortex with the lower centers, i.e. the lower sensory and motor neurons in the spinal cord or brainstem.

Fiber content by part

PartContents
Anterior limbFibers connecting the cortex with basal ganglia, cerebellum, thalamus and reticular formation, and finally the corticonuclear tract.
GenuCortico-bulbar tract.
Posterior limb: anterior 2/3Cortico-spinal tract mixed with extrapyramidal fibers.
Posterior limb: posterior halfSensory radiation from the thalamus (PVLNT) to the sensory areas, mainly areas 3, 1, 2 and 5, 7.
Sub-lenticular partAuditory radiation to the auditory cortex.
Retro-lenticular partOptic radiation to the visual cortex.

Blood supply and clinical relevance

  • Supplied mainly by the lenticulostriate artery, a branch of the middle cerebral artery.
  • This artery is most liable to hemorrhage and thrombosis because it takes a sharp acute angle in its course.
  • Because of the fiber arrangement in the posterior limb, paralysis of the upper limb is more severe than of the lower limb, and motor functions are affected more than sensory ones.

Upper motor neuron lesion (UMNL)

Definition: a lesion that interrupts the connection between the upper motor neuron (UMN) and the lower motor neuron (LMN), i.e. any lesion above the anterior horn cells or above the motor nuclei of cranial nerves in the brainstem.

  • UMN: in the motor and premotor areas of the cerebral cortex and other brainstem centers.
  • LMN: in the anterior horn cells of the spinal cord (limbs and trunk muscles) and in the brainstem (head and neck muscles); their axons form the motor nerves to skeletal muscles.

Causes

  • Internal capsule lesion (the most common cause): hemorrhage or thrombosis of the lenticulostriate artery.
  • Vascular lesion in area 4 of the cortex, secondary to tumors or trauma.
  • Vascular thrombosis of the medullary pyramid, which destroys mainly the pyramidal tract and spares the extrapyramidal.
  • Complete transection or hemisection of the spinal cord, affecting muscles whose centers lie below the lesion.

Characters (internal capsule lesion)

  • Spastic paralysis: loss of voluntary movements, widespread over the opposite half of the body (hemiplegia).
  • Hypertonia of muscle tone.
  • Deep reflexes (tendon jerks) are exaggerated and ankle clonus may appear.
  • Superficial reflexes (abdominal; cremasteric in males) are inhibited, due to loss of supraspinal facilitation or to rigidity. The plantar reflex becomes Babinski's sign.
  • Muscle wasting is not marked: the muscle still contracts reflexly, its motor neuron centers are intact, and its blood flow and metabolism are undisturbed.

Why hypertonia occurs in internal capsule lesions: (1) the vestibular nucleus, which facilitates tone, lies below the capsule and stays intact; (2) the inhibitory medullary reticular formation becomes inactive because it depends on inhibitory fibers from higher cortical centers that are destroyed; (3) the facilitatory pontine reticular formation has intrinsic activity and nothing inhibits it.

Some UMNL cause hypotonia instead: a pure vascular lesion in area 4, or a lesion of the medullary pyramid.

Special features in internal capsule UMNL

  • The face is little affected: only the lower part on the opposite side, so the patient cannot show his teeth or whistle. Some ipsilateral fibers supply the brainstem motor nuclei (bilateral innervation).
  • Abdominal and thoracic muscles and sphincters are spared, as they are doubly innervated from both pyramidal tracts.

Lower motor neuron lesion (LMNL)

Definition: a lesion that destroys the reflex arc of the muscle: the anterior horn cells (e.g. poliomyelitis), the motor nerve (neuritis, trauma), or the muscle itself (myopathies).

  • Flaccid paralysis, restricted to one limb or a group of muscles.
  • Complete loss of deep reflexes (tendon jerk).
  • Superficial reflexes remain intact as long as their reflex arcs are unaffected.
  • Marked muscle atrophy (disuse atrophy).
  • No clonus and no Babinski's sign.
  • Reactions of degeneration: loss of excitability with prolonged chronaxie; the muscle stops responding to faradic current (only galvanic); fibrillation (asynchronous rapid invisible contractions in a single fiber, 2-10/second) due to denervation hypersensitivity to ACh; anodal closing contraction stronger than cathodal closing contraction (ACC > CCC; normally CCC > ACC).

Basal ganglia

Functional anatomy

  • Nuclear masses of grey matter in the central core of the white matter of the cerebral hemispheres, separating the cerebral cortex from the diencephalon; the main nuclei lie lateral to the thalamus.
  • Three large masses: caudate nucleus, putamen, globus pallidus. Corpus striatum = caudate + putamen; lentiform nucleus = putamen + globus pallidus.
  • Related nuclei: subthalamic nuclei, substantia nigra, parts of the thalamus, red nucleus.
  • Functions are purely motor; they form the chief part of the extrapyramidal system.
  • They give no direct descending tracts to spinal motor nuclei, but act indirectly through brainstem centers (reticular formation, vestibular and olivary nuclei). Their lesions therefore cause no paralysis but disturbances of muscle tone and abnormal involuntary movements.

Connections

Afferent:

  • Cortico-striate projection from nearly all parts of the cortex to the corpus striatum: facilitatory on the putamen and inhibitory on the caudate.
  • Cortico-striato-pallido-thalamo-cortical connection: frontal association areas to caudate, then globus pallidus, then ventrolateral thalamic nuclei (same side), and lastly the motor and premotor areas.
  • Centromedian nucleus of the thalamus to the corpus striatum.

Efferent:

  • The main efferent is from the globus pallidus back to the cortex, mainly the motor and premotor areas.
  • Short circuits between the nuclei, including dopaminergic nigrostriatal fibers and GABA-ergic striatum-to-substantia nigra projections (nigro-striatal dopaminergic feedback circuit).
  • Striatum to superior colliculus; globus pallidus to brainstem centers (vestibular, red nucleus, inferior olivary nucleus, reticular formation).

Functions

  • In birds and cats they are the chief motor center for voluntary movement; in humans they act in association with the cortico-spinal system.
  • Control of subconscious gross postural movements (corpus striatum).
  • Cognitive function: they regulate the linkage between sensory input about a movement and the information already stored about its performance.
  • Globus pallidus: may be responsible for the posture taken during particular voluntary movements.
  • Planning and programming of voluntary movement, linking the frontal association area to the motor cortex through the thalamus.
  • The corpus striatum is inhibitory to muscle tone.
  • Inhibitory circuit (cortico-striato-pallido-thalamo-cortical): links the suppressor areas (4S, 19S, 25S) with the basal ganglia through the thalamus; it inhibits high activity of the motor and premotor areas and prevents abnormal involuntary movements.

Physiological characters

  • They receive almost all their input from the cerebral cortex and return almost all their output to it.
  • Almost all motor and sensory fibers between cortex and spinal cord pass between the caudate nucleus and putamen.
  • Very high oxygen consumption and high copper content.
  • Transmitters include ACh, dopamine, GABA, serotonin and norepinephrine.
  • Many neurons discharge mainly during slow steady movements, not rapid ones.

Lesions

  • Causes: reduced blood flow (atherosclerosis, aging); depletion of transmitters, especially dopamine; excessive use of drugs that interfere with transmitter synthesis (phenothiazine derivatives); rheumatic fever in children (Sydenham chorea); degenerative CNS lesions.
  • Diseases: Parkinson's syndrome (paralysis agitans), chorea, athetosis, ballismus.

Rigidity versus spasticity

FeatureRigiditySpasticity
OriginExtrapyramidal, mostly corpus striatumMostly internal capsule lesion (UMNL)
CauseIncreased discharge from alpha neuronsIncreased discharge from gamma neurons
CharacterCog-wheel or lead pipeClasp-knife
Clonus / BabinskiAbsentPresent
MovementsUsually with involuntary movementsUsually loss of voluntary movements

Key Points / Quick Review

Motor neurons

  • Alpha: extrafusal, 70%. Gamma: intrafusal, 30%. Lateral horn: autonomic.

Internal capsule

  • Genu: cortico-bulbar. Posterior limb: corticospinal (anterior 2/3), sensory radiation (posterior half).
  • Sub-lenticular: auditory; retro-lenticular: optic radiation.
  • Lenticulostriate artery (MCA): acute angle, prone to hemorrhage.
  • Upper limb worse than lower; motor worse than sensory.

UMNL

  • Spastic hemiplegia, hypertonia, exaggerated deep reflexes, clonus, Babinski.
  • Little wasting; lower face only; trunk muscles and sphincters spared.
  • Hypotonia in pure area 4 or pyramid lesions.

LMNL

  • Flaccid paralysis, absent deep reflexes, marked atrophy, no Babinski.
  • Reactions of degeneration: fibrillation, ACC > CCC.

Basal ganglia

  • Caudate, putamen, globus pallidus; extrapyramidal and purely motor.
  • Input from cortex, main output from globus pallidus back to cortex.
  • Lesions: tone disturbance and involuntary movements, not paralysis.
  • Diseases: Parkinson's, chorea, athetosis, ballismus.

Rigidity vs spasticity

  • Rigidity: alpha, cog-wheel/lead pipe, striatal. Spasticity: gamma, clasp-knife, internal capsule, clonus and Babinski.
